**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the hardware we already own? My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should commit a focused four-to-six-week effort to measurement, scheduling, batching, model routing, and workload shaping, with a predefined threshold that would justify a purchase if utilisation improvements do not close the gap. This is not a blanket “do more with less” position; it is a sequencing decision based on cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility.

The direct cost of new hardware is the easiest part to see and, in some ways, the least important. A incremental purchase is not just the sticker price of accelerators. It includes host machines, networking, power, cooling, rack space, spare capacity, maintenance, firmware and driver compatibility work, and the operational burden of another failure domain. Even if the capital expense is approved quickly, procurement and installation can take weeks or months, during which the current constraints remain. There is also a recurring cost in engineering attention: every new hardware generation or vendor configuration introduces another matrix of kernels, container images, memory profiles, and monitoring exceptions. If our current fleet is poorly understood, adding capacity risks multiplying inefficiency rather than solving it.

Utilisation work has its own cost, but it is mostly engineering time and organisational discipline. That time is not free. The team could otherwise be improving model quality, reducing product latency, hardening evaluation pipelines, or shipping user-facing features. This is the central opportunity cost, and it should be taken seriously. A utilisation project that becomes an open-ended infrastructure rewrite would be a bad trade. To avoid that, the effort should be bounded, instrumented, and tied to concrete service outcomes. We are not trying to build a perfect scheduler; we are trying to determine whether the existing fleet can meet the next two quarters of demand with acceptable latency and reliability.

Latency is where the decision becomes more subtle. Buying hardware can reduce queueing delay by adding parallelism, but only if the workload is actually queued behind insufficient compute. If our tail latency is driven by cold starts, inefficient batching, model loading, memory fragmentation, synchronous preprocessing, or poorly chosen concurrency limits, more accelerators will not fix the user experience. In some cases, additional hardware can even make latency worse by spreading requests across more devices and increasing orchestration overhead. Better utilisation, by contrast, can improve both throughput and latency when it reduces idle gaps, avoids unnecessary model swaps, keeps hot models resident, and routes small interactive requests separately from large batch jobs. The key is to distinguish interactive service-level objectives from offline experimentation and bulk inference. A single undifferentiated capacity pool tends to make both classes of work unreliable.

Reliability also favours understanding before expansion. Our current reliability problems are not obviously capacity shortages; they appear to be coupled to contention, retries, and uneven workload placement. When a long-running evaluation job occupies a device needed for interactive inference, the system may remain “up” while the product is effectively degraded. More hardware would provide more blast-radius separation, but so would better admission control, quotas, priority queues, and workload isolation. A larger fleet also increases the number of components that can fail, and it can mask software defects by providing slack until demand grows into the new capacity. Utilisation work should include failure-mode clarity: what happens when a device is lost, when a model fails to load, when a batch times out, or when a high-priority request arrives during a saturated window. If we cannot answer those questions for the current fleet, we will not answer them better with more devices.

Reversibility is perhaps the strongest argument for the recommendation. Engineering improvements to observability, scheduling, batching, and routing are largely reversible and portable. If we later buy hardware, those improvements continue to pay off by reducing the amount we need to buy and by making the new capacity easier to operate. If we buy first and later discover that the bottleneck was software or workload design, the purchase is only partially reversible. Hardware can be repurposed, resold, or used for training and experimentation, but the capital allocation, integration effort, and operational complexity are sunk. A delayed purchase is usually cheaper than a premature one, provided the delay is bounded by evidence rather than indecision.

There is real uncertainty here. Demand may grow faster than our forecasts, especially if a new product workflow lands or if model context lengths increase. Utilisation improvements may yield less than expected if the fleet is already close to its practical ceiling. Some latency targets may require dedicated devices rather than clever scheduling. Vendor lead times may lengthen, making a later purchase more painful. We should therefore define purchase triggers now: sustained saturation during business-critical windows after optimisation, tail latency that remains above target under realistic load, insufficient headroom for a single-device failure, or a committed product requirement that cannot be met by workload shaping. These triggers should be measured, not debated from anecdotes.

The practical path is to instrument the current fleet for a short baseline period, separate interactive and batch workloads, introduce priority-aware scheduling and batching, reduce model reloads, and run load tests that reflect production traffic. At the end of the period, we should compare cost per accepted request, p50 and p99 latency, failure behaviour under device loss, and available headroom. If those numbers meet the agreed thresholds, we defer purchase. If they do not, we buy with a much clearer specification of what is needed and why.

For now, the better decision is to improve utilisation first. It preserves capital, protects engineering focus through a bounded scope, improves latency and reliability where they are most likely originating, and keeps our options open. Buying more hardware remains a valid next step, but it should be a response to measured constraints rather than a substitute for understanding them.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the machines we already own? My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should commit a focused four-to-six-week effort to measurement, scheduling, batching, model routing, and workload shaping, with a pre-defined threshold that would justify a purchase if utilisation improvements do not close the gap. This is not a blanket “do more with less” position; it is a sequencing decision based on cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility.

The direct cost of new hardware is the easiest part to see and, in some ways, the least important. A incremental purchase is not just the sticker price of accelerators. It includes host machines, power, cooling, rack space, networking, storage bandwidth, spare capacity, warranty handling, and the operational tax of another hardware generation in the fleet. Even if the capital expense is approved quickly, procurement and deployment can take long enough that the bottleneck may have changed by the time the machines are online. More importantly, buying hardware converts a flexible engineering problem into a fixed asset. If our demand is spiky, poorly instrumented, or driven by a few inefficient workflows, additional capacity may simply hide the underlying issue while raising our baseline burn.

Utilisation work has its own cost, of course. It consumes the time of exactly the people who are currently being asked to ship product features, improve model quality, and support customers. That opportunity cost is real and should not be dismissed. However, the work is likely to produce durable benefits even if we later buy more hardware: better queueing, clearer service-level objectives, more predictable batching, fewer idle reservations, and a better understanding of which jobs truly require local execution. Those improvements compound. By contrast, buying hardware first leaves us with the same scheduling pathologies, the same unclear workload taxonomy, and the same inability to explain why a given request waited twelve minutes for a GPU that was nominally available.

Latency is the strongest argument for more capacity, and we should take it seriously. If interactive workloads are missing user-facing targets, no amount of elegant utilisation theory will make a saturated system feel fast. But latency is not only a function of aggregate FLOPs. In our current environment, a meaningful share of delay appears to come from queue placement, model loading, cold caches, oversized contexts, unnecessary precision, and jobs that are treated as urgent by default. We should separate tail latency for interactive inference from throughput for offline evaluation, fine-tuning, embedding generation, and experimentation. A system that is “at capacity” may actually be suffering from priority inversion rather than insufficient compute. Before buying, we need to know whether the painful waits are caused by physical saturation or by policy.

Reliability also cuts both ways. More machines can improve redundancy and reduce the blast radius of a single node failure, especially if we have enough spare capacity to drain and repair hosts without degrading service. But a larger fleet also introduces more failure domains, more driver and firmware variance, more networking complexity, and more chances for subtle performance regressions. If our current reliability problems are rooted in ad hoc allocation, manual pinning, or jobs that fail after holding devices for hours, then utilisation work is reliability work. A scheduler that enforces time limits, health checks, preemption rules, and clean retry semantics may do more for availability than another rack of accelerators. We should be careful not to solve software fragility with hardware abundance.

The opportunity cost of buying now is not merely financial. Every hour spent integrating new nodes is an hour not spent reducing inference cost per request, improving observability, or deciding which workloads can be moved to smaller models, CPU paths, remote bursts, or asynchronous execution. There is also a strategic cost: once hardware arrives, teams naturally shape their designs around its existence. That can be good, but it can also lock us into local-first assumptions when a hybrid approach would be more resilient and economical. Conversely, the opportunity cost of delaying purchase is that product teams may continue to experience slow iteration, and we may miss a window where capacity enables a valuable experiment. That risk is real, which is why the utilisation effort should be time-boxed rather than open-ended.

Reversibility favours improving utilisation first. Software and process changes can be rolled back, tuned, or redirected. A hardware purchase is only partially reversible, and resale value, internal chargeback politics, and deployment lead times make it a heavier commitment. We can also stage the decision: define the metrics that matter, instrument the current fleet, implement the highest-confidence improvements, and then reassess. If, after that, interactive p95 latency remains above target during normal demand, sustained utilisation stays high after batching and scheduling fixes, and reliability still requires more spare headroom, then buying hardware becomes a well-supported decision rather than a reflex.

The uncertainty here is substantial. We do not yet have a clean model of demand growth, and some upcoming product work could change the mix of workloads dramatically. Model architecture changes may reduce or increase memory pressure. Vendor pricing and availability may move. A major customer commitment could make dedicated capacity rational even at low average utilisation. We should therefore avoid pretending that a utilisation project will definitively answer every capacity question. It will, however, replace anecdotes with evidence and give us a much better basis for deciding how much to buy, what kind to buy, and when.

My recommendation is to pause new local hardware procurement for one focused improvement cycle, with explicit success criteria agreed in advance: latency by workload class, sustained and peak utilisation, queue wait time, job failure and retry rates, cost per completed workload, and engineer time spent on capacity firefighting. At the end of that cycle, we should either declare the fleet sufficient for the next planning horizon or place a scoped purchase tied to the specific bottleneck that remains. This approach respects the urgency of latency and reliability without letting urgency force an irreversible decision. It also preserves the option to buy later with better information, which is usually the cheapest option we have.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Platform and Applied AI Teams  
**From:** Engineering Strategy  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better  
**Date:** 2026-07-14  

We need to make a near-term decision about local AI capacity. The question in front of us is deceptively simple: should we purchase additional GPUs and supporting infrastructure, or should we invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the hardware we already own? My recommendation is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should first commit to a focused utilisation programme, with a defined review point, because our current constraints appear to be at least as much scheduling, observability, and workload-shape problems as they are raw compute problems. That said, this is not a claim that hardware is unnecessary; it is a claim that buying now would likely lock in cost and complexity before we have extracted the cheaper, more reversible gains available in our existing fleet.

The cost case for delaying purchase is strong, but it is not merely about avoiding capital expense. Additional accelerators bring a stack of committed costs: servers, power, cooling, rack space, network upgrades, spare capacity, firmware and driver maintenance, and the operational burden of keeping another pool of devices healthy. Even when the sticker price of the cards dominates the conversation, the durable cost is the whole system around them. More importantly, hardware purchases convert flexible engineering budget into fixed capacity. If our workload mix changes—smaller models, more batch inference, more aggressive quantisation, greater use of hosted APIs for burst work, or a shift from experimentation to steady-state serving—the new hardware may sit underused or be optimised for the wrong bottleneck. The opportunity cost is the engineering work we do not fund because the budget has become silicon: better batching, caching, admission control, model compilation, queue policies, and evaluation tooling. Those improvements tend to compound across whatever hardware we own, and many remain useful if we later expand.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side. When teams experience slow iteration, unpredictable queue times, or missed internal demo windows, the intuitive answer is more capacity. There is truth in this. If GPUs are saturated with useful work at most hours, additional hardware reduces contention and gives us lower tail latency. But our current telemetry does not yet show a clean capacity-limited story. We see high instantaneous utilisation on some nodes alongside idle memory, fragmented allocation, long-lived development sessions holding devices, and jobs that are poorly packed because they request whole accelerators for workloads that could share them. We also see batch jobs competing with interactive work under the same scheduling policy. In that environment, buying more hardware may reduce average wait time while leaving the underlying variance intact. A better scheduler, separate queues for interactive and batch work, time-slicing for development, and stronger defaults for memory limits could improve perceived latency without increasing the fleet. The key distinction is whether latency comes from insufficient throughput or from poor isolation and prioritisation. At present, the evidence points to a mixture, with isolation and policy being material contributors.

Reliability also cuts both ways. More hardware can improve resilience by adding redundancy and reducing the blast radius of a failed node. It can also reduce reliability by expanding the number of components that must be monitored, patched, and diagnosed. Local AI clusters fail in mundane ways: driver mismatches, thermal throttling, bad cables, stale container images, partial memory errors, and jobs that leave devices in awkward states. Adding nodes without first improving fleet hygiene multiplies those failure modes. Utilisation work, by contrast, usually forces us to build the operational foundations we need anyway: accurate inventory, health checks, job provenance, preemption behaviour, checkpointing, and capacity dashboards. These make the current fleet more reliable and make any future expansion safer. If we do buy later, we will be buying into a system that can absorb the hardware rather than one that merely accumulates it.

The hardest part of the decision is uncertainty. We do not have perfect attribution of demand. Some teams are deliberately conservative about reporting future needs because they do not want to be queue-bound; others overestimate because current waits make every project feel capacity-constrained. Product plans may introduce new multimodal workloads that are genuinely throughput-heavy. Model quality requirements may limit quantisation or force larger context windows. Hosted inference may become cheaper, or it may become unacceptable for privacy and cost reasons. We should acknowledge that a utilisation-first programme could delay a purchase that, in hindsight, was obviously needed. The way to manage that is not to pretend the uncertainty away, but to set a short, explicit decision horizon. Over the next six to eight weeks, we should instrument the fleet more carefully, classify workloads by latency sensitivity, introduce queue separation, enforce release of idle development sessions, improve batching and model warm-start behaviour, and publish weekly capacity and wait-time metrics. At the end of that period, if sustained useful utilisation remains above a defined threshold and interactive tail latency still violates our target, we should buy.

Reversibility favours this sequence. Engineering improvements to scheduling, observability, and workload packaging are largely reversible and portable. If they do not work, we can roll back policies, adjust defaults, or redirect effort. If they do work, they reduce the size and urgency of any future purchase. Hardware acquisition is much less reversible: it is slow to procure, hard to return, and creates organisational pressure to justify its use. There is also a subtle behavioural risk. Adding capacity often relaxes the discipline that would have produced better system design. Teams stop batching, stop cleaning up sessions, and stop measuring because the immediate pain disappears. We should be careful not to purchase our way out of information.

My recommendation, then, is to pause additional local AI hardware purchases for one utilisation cycle, while preparing a procurement path so we can move quickly if the data justifies it. We should treat this as a capacity decision, not an austerity measure. The goal is to buy the right amount at the right time, with confidence that the bottleneck is truly compute. In the meantime, we should assign clear ownership to the utilisation work and define success in terms of queue latency, sustained useful utilisation, job failure rate, and engineer wait time. If those metrics do not improve materially, or if demand grows faster than expected, we should expand the fleet without hesitation. But buying now would spend money, operational attention, and strategic flexibility before we know whether our problem is too little hardware or too little control over the hardware we already have.
